# Tests That Guard the Repository

Put the promises the *repository* makes into the same suite as the code, so they fail on the same
command. Fifteen of [[agent-orchestrator]]'s 145 [[pytest]] units never import the product: they read
files.

## What they assert

| Guard | Fails when |
|---|---|
| version consistency | any of the six places carrying the version disagrees — manifest, changelog heading, skill bundle, install line, front door, docs |
| dependency claims | the extension gains a runtime dependency, or the backend a second one |
| commands | a command is contributed in the manifest but never registered |
| packaging | the `.vsix` would include something that must not ship |
| secrets | an API-key-shaped string appears anywhere in the tree |
| paths | a developer's absolute path is committed |
| links | any relative markdown link in the docs resolves to nothing |
| runners | `make` and the PowerShell script stop offering the same targets |

## Why these and not a linter

Each one is a promise already written down somewhere in prose. "The version appears in six places" is
a line in the release procedure; without this guard it is a line someone has to remember at 1 a.m.
The test does not add a rule — it makes an existing rule enforceable, which is the difference between
a convention and a constraint.

The dead-link guard is the clearest case. Documentation cross-references rot silently and are found by
a reader, not by an author — [[documentation-drift]]. Two broken ADR links were sitting in the
architecture document when this test was written; it found them, and it will find the next two.

## Cost, honestly

They are slower to write than they look, because each one has to decide what *counts*: the secret
scanner must match key shapes without matching the documentation that discusses keys, and the link
checker must strip anchors and skip `http`, `https` and `mailto`. A guard with a false positive gets
deleted by the next person in a hurry, so the tuning is the work.

They also only cover what is committed. A test cannot tell you the vendor renamed a CLI flag —
that is stated as uncovered rather than papered over.
